title: Clinical Radiology
description: Choosing and interpreting imaging: chest and abdominal radiographs, musculoskeletal imaging, neuroimaging, emergency and interventional radiology, and radiation protection for clinicians.

topics.title: Chest Radiograph Interpretation
topics.summary: Systematic review, common patterns: consolidation, collapse, effusion, pneumothorax, TB and heart failure.

notes.b: Check patient details, date, projection (PA preferred — AP magnifies the heart), rotation (spinous processes midway between the clavicle heads), inspiration (about 6 anterior or 10 posterior ribs above the diaphragm) and penetration. Then review: airway (trachea central), breathing (lung fields, pleura, costophrenic angles), cardiac (cardiothoracic ratio > 0.5 on PA suggests cardiomegaly; borders), diaphragm (right usually higher; free air under the diaphragm), and everything else — bones, soft tissues, lines and tubes, and 'review areas' (apices, behind the heart, hila, below the diaphragm). The silhouette sign: loss of a normal border indicates adjacent pathology (right heart border — right middle lobe; left heart border — lingula; hemidiaphragm — lower lobe).

Consolidation: airspace opacification with air bronchograms (pneumonia). Collapse (atelectasis): volume loss with displacement of fissures, trachea and mediastinum towards the affected side (e.g. sail sign of left lower lobe collapse behind the heart). Pleural effusion: blunted costophrenic angle, meniscus sign; large effusions push the mediastinum away. Pneumothorax: visible pleural edge without lung markings beyond; tension pneumothorax shifts the mediastinum away (clinical diagnosis — don't wait for X-ray). Pulmonary TB: upper-zone infiltrates, cavitation, fibrosis with volume loss, hilar lymphadenopathy (primary), miliary pattern (tiny nodules throughout — disseminated); atypical appearances in HIV. Heart failure: cardiomegaly, upper lobe venous diversion, Kerley B lines, bat-wing alveolar oedema and effusions (ABCDE mnemonic: Alveolar oedema, kerley B lines, Cardiomegaly, Dilated upper lobe vessels, Effusions). Mass lesions: lung cancer, metastases ('cannonball'), and pneumoconiosis in miners.

topics.title: Abdominal and Genitourinary Imaging
topics.summary: Abdominal X-rays, ultrasound and CT in the acute abdomen, urinary tract imaging.

notes.b: An erect chest X-ray shows free intraperitoneal air under the diaphragm (perforated viscus — peptic ulcer, typhoid perforation). The supine abdominal X-ray assesses bowel obstruction (dilated small bowel > 3 cm with valvulae conniventes, centrally; large bowel > 6 cm (caecum > 9 cm) with haustra, peripherally), volvulus (sigmoid — coffee bean; caecal), and some stones and calcifications (about 90% of renal stones are radio-opaque; gallstones mostly not). Rigler's sign (both sides of the bowel wall visible) indicates pneumoperitoneum. Ultrasound is first-line for right upper quadrant pain (gallstones, cholecystitis), pelvic pain in women (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian pathology), children (intussusception — target sign; appendicitis) and the FAST scan in trauma. CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast is the most useful test for undifferentiated acute abdomen in adults (appendicitis, diverticulitis, perforation, abscess, pancreatitis complications, bowel ischaemia, and cancer staging).
k: SB > 3 cm; LB > 6 cm; caecum > 9 cm

notes.b: Renal colic: non-contrast CT KUB is the most sensitive test (detects nearly all stones); ultrasound (hydronephrosis) is preferred in pregnancy and children. Ultrasound assesses kidney size and echogenicity (small echogenic kidneys — chronic kidney disease), hydronephrosis, cysts and masses, bladder (wall thickening and calcification in schistosomiasis; post-void residual) and prostate volume. Intravenous urography (IVU) is largely replaced by CT urography (haematuria workup — urothelial tumours). Micturating cystourethrography (MCU) shows vesicoureteric reflux and posterior urethral valves in boys; retrograde urethrography (RUG) evaluates urethral strictures (common in Nigerian men) and trauma. Contrast safety: check renal function and allergy history before iodinated contrast.

topics.title: Musculoskeletal Imaging
topics.summary: Fracture imaging, bone infections and tumours, sickle cell bone disease and spine imaging.

notes.b: Fracture imaging requires two views at right angles and inclusion of the joints above and below (rule of twos: two views, two joints, two occasions if needed, two limbs in children for comparison). Some fractures are occult initially (scaphoid, hip — MRI or CT). Paediatric fractures: greenstick, buckle (torus), and growth plate injuries (Salter–Harris classification I–V; higher grades risk growth disturbance). Osteomyelitis: plain films are normal for the first 10–14 days, then show periosteal reaction, lytic areas, sequestrum (dense dead bone) and involucrum (new bone); MRI detects early changes. Septic arthritis: ultrasound shows effusion to guide aspiration. Sickle cell bone disease: avascular necrosis of the femoral head (flattening, sclerosis), H-shaped vertebrae, bone infarcts, dactylitis in infants and Salmonella osteomyelitis. Spinal TB (Pott's disease): disc space narrowing with destruction of adjacent vertebral end plates, paravertebral abscess and gibbus — MRI is best.

Features of aggressive bone lesions: wide zone of transition, permeative or moth-eaten destruction, cortical breakthrough, aggressive periosteal reaction (sunburst, Codman's triangle, onion-skin) and soft-tissue mass. Primary tumours by age: osteosarcoma (adolescents, metaphysis around the knee — sunburst and Codman's triangle), Ewing sarcoma (children, diaphysis — onion-skin periosteal reaction), giant cell tumour (young adults, epiphysis extending to articular surface), and multiple myeloma (older adults — punched-out lytic lesions, 'pepper-pot' skull). Metastases (breast, prostate — sclerotic; lung, kidney, thyroid — lytic) are the commonest bone tumours in adults; bone scintigraphy detects them. Rickets: cupped, frayed metaphyses and widened growth plates; osteoporosis: reduced density and fragility fractures (DEXA). Burkitt lymphoma causes jaw bone destruction with loss of lamina dura in children.

topics.title: Neuroimaging and Emergency Radiology
topics.summary: CT in head injury and stroke, MRI indications, and imaging in trauma.

notes.b: Non-contrast CT head is the first test for head injury, suspected stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and acute neurological deterioration. Acute blood is hyperdense: extradural haematoma (biconvex, limited by sutures), subdural haematoma (crescentic, crosses sutures; chronic subdurals are hypodense), subarachnoid haemorrhage (blood in cisterns and sulci), and intracerebral haemorrhage. Early ischaemic stroke may be normal or show subtle loss of grey–white differentiation and a hyperdense artery sign; infarcts become hypodense after 24 hours. Signs of raised intracranial pressure: effaced sulci and cisterns, midline shift, hydrocephalus. CT indications after head injury include GCS < 13 initially or < 15 at 2 hours, suspected skull fracture, seizures, vomiting more than once, focal deficit, and anticoagulation. MRI is superior for posterior fossa lesions, demyelination, tumours, infection (abscess, encephalitis), spinal cord compression and early stroke (diffusion-weighted imaging). Ring-enhancing lesions: abscess, toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, metastases and glioma.
k: Early stroke CT may be normal

notes.b: In major trauma, imaging supports but must not delay resuscitation: chest and pelvic X-rays and FAST in the resuscitation room, then whole-body CT ('trauma CT') for stable patients. Cervical spine imaging: CT is preferred in adults with high-risk mechanisms; clinical decision rules (NEXUS, Canadian C-spine rule) identify who needs imaging. Lateral C-spine X-ray must show C1 to the C7/T1 junction. Pelvic fractures (open-book) cause major haemorrhage — pelvic binder. Aortic injury (widened mediastinum). CT angiography identifies active bleeding; interventional radiology can embolise bleeding vessels (splenic, pelvic, bronchial arteries for haemoptysis, postpartum haemorrhage). Other interventional procedures: image-guided biopsies and drainages (liver abscess, empyema, obstructed kidney — nephrostomy), angioplasty and stenting, TIPS, and biliary drainage. Nigeria has growing but limited interventional radiology capacity.

topics.title: Choosing Imaging Wisely and Radiation Protection
topics.summary: Appropriate requests, radiation doses, imaging in pregnancy and children, and contrast safety.

notes.b: A good imaging request states the clinical question, relevant history and examination, and how the result will change management. Justification is the first principle of radiation protection: an exposure must do more good than harm. Choose the test that answers the question with least radiation — ultrasound and MRI use no ionising radiation. Referral guidelines (e.g. iRefer, ACR Appropriateness Criteria) help clinicians choose. Unnecessary imaging (e.g. routine skull X-rays for head injury — CT is better; lumbar spine X-rays in non-specific back pain without red flags) wastes resources and exposes patients. Approximate effective doses: chest X-ray 0.02 mSv (a few days of background radiation), lumbar spine X-ray ~1 mSv, CT head ~2 mSv, CT abdomen–pelvis ~8–10 mSv (years of background); natural background is about 2–3 mSv per year. Radiation risk (stochastic — cancer) is higher in children.
k: US and MRI: no ionising radiation

notes.b: Pregnancy: ask all women of reproductive age about pregnancy before abdominal/pelvic exposures (10-day rule/28-day rule practices); prefer ultrasound or MRI; if CT is necessary (e.g. trauma, suspected PE), the benefit usually outweighs the small risk — doses below 50–100 mGy are not associated with fetal malformations. Children: use child-sized protocols (ALARA — as low as reasonably achievable), ultrasound first where possible. Iodinated contrast: check renal function (eGFR), history of prior reactions, asthma and metformin use; hydrate at-risk patients; manage reactions (anaphylaxis — IM adrenaline). Gadolinium in MRI: caution in severe renal impairment (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis). Clinicians should also protect themselves in fluoroscopy (lead aprons, distance, shielding) and follow NNRA regulations.
